title: HAPS: Hierarchical LLM Routing with Joint Architecture and Parameter Search
claim: Prior routers pick only among fixed discrete options; ours also searches continuous parameters, so the best choice can change.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels plus bottom example row; curved expansion arrow between panels
description: The figure is split into a left panel, "Traditional Approach: Discrete Architecture Routing" (green), and a right panel, "Our Approach: Joint Architecture & Parameter Routing" (blue). In each panel, four LLM logos (Mistral, Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek) feed into a labeled search space and then a router box. On the right the logos are paired with colored slider icons for parameters. The router fans out to five task icons: Conversation, Coding, Computer Use, Trip Planning and Movie Recommendation. A curved arrow labeled "Search Space Expansion" sits between the panels. A bottom "Illustrative Example: Conversation Task Adaptation" strip shows the traditional router selecting Qwen with fixed parameters, while ours selects Mistral with proper parameters. A legend row runs along the very bottom.
caption: Illustration of the traditional LLM router versus our proposed model. Unlike standard methods that only select architectures, our framework jointly routes both LLM architectures and their specific parameters, so the preferred architecture may change once its parameters can adapt.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing aims to exploit the specialized strengths of different LLMs for diverse tasks. However, existing approaches typically focus only on selecting LLM architectures, treating candidate models as fixed while overlooking parameter adaptation, which can substantially affect task performance. In this paper, we introduce HAPS, a hierarchical LLM routing framework that jointly searches over model architectures and parameters. Specifically, a high-level router selects among candidate LLM architectures, while a low-level router generates input-conditioned LoRA parameters for the selected architecture, expanding each candidate from a single fixed behavior into a region of reachable behaviors. The low-level router is built on the backbone of the high-level router, so that architecture selection and parameter generation share a common representation of the prompt. We further optimize the whole framework with a reinforcement learning objective. Extensive experiments show that HAPS consistently outperforms strong routing baselines across reasoning- and knowledge-intensive benchmarks, with analyses of its components, design choices, scalability, cost, and mixed open- and closed-source deployment further demonstrating the robustness of these gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/zihangtian/HAPS.
